name: Interview Transcription and Speaker Separation
title: Interview Transcription and Speaker Separation
answer: Interview transcription and speaker separation covers the conversion of recorded speech into written text and the attribution of each stretch of that text to the person who spoke it. In qualitative and mixed methods work it sits at the front of the analysis pipeline, before coding, memoing or thematic work begins. The topic spans one-to-one interviews, focus groups, multi-party meetings and oral history recordings, where turns overlap and speakers are not always known in advance. It stops short of interpretation, because a speaker-labelled transcript is evidence about who said what, not a finding about what it means.

sections.body: Interview transcription and speaker separation covers the conversion of recorded speech into written text and the attribution of each stretch of that text to the person who spoke it. In qualitative and mixed methods work it sits at the front of the analysis pipeline, before coding, memoing or thematic work begins. The topic spans one-to-one interviews, focus groups, multi-party meetings and oral history recordings, where turns overlap and speakers are not always known in advance. It stops short of interpretation, because a speaker-labelled transcript is evidence about who said what, not a finding about what it means.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on audio capture and storage first, since the quality of the recording sets the ceiling for everything downstream. Practitioners typically use a local machine or a cloud service, a speech recognition model, a speaker diarization model and a transcript editor, with a GPU speeding up batch processing and a CPU-only laptop handling short files. Model and tool catalogues on this site run to 800 scientific models and 732 AI tools, and speech and diarization models appear among them. Consent records, retention schedules and a place to keep the original audio alongside the derived text are part of the setup.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical pass begins with audio cleaning and segmentation, then automatic speech recognition to produce a raw transcript, then diarization to mark speaker turns, then alignment of the two so each utterance carries a speaker label and a timestamp. Well known tools in this space include Whisper for recognition and pyannote for diarization, while qualitative packages such as NVivo, MAXQDA and ELAN handle coding, synchronisation and review of the labelled text. Human correction follows, because names, numbers, dialect, crosstalk and overlapping speech are where automatic output fails most often. Teams usually fix a transcription convention in advance, verbatim or lightly edited, and record how disagreements between coders were resolved. Where a study reports reliability, it is normally computed on the corrected transcript rather than the raw machine output.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on consent, voice as personal data, and the terms under which a vendor processes recordings. Voice can count as biometric data under regimes such as the GDPR, and health or criminal justice interviews attract stricter handling, so retention limits, encryption and deletion schedules matter as much as accuracy. Cloud transcription raises cross-border transfer questions and the risk that a service trains on submitted audio, which is why many teams check the contract before uploading. Accuracy risk is uneven, since accents, code-switching, hearing difficulties and overlapping speakers produce errors that can silently change who is quoted. Provenance means recording which model, version and settings produced the transcript, when the human correction happened, and where the audio is stored. Where this site cites work on the topic, it links to the original paper rather than to a search tool.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Work on the topic is moving toward better handling of overlapping speech, code-switching and long multi-party recordings, which are the cases where diarization still struggles. On-device and locally hosted models are becoming more practical, which reduces the need to send sensitive audio to a third party. Tighter integration between transcription output and qualitative analysis software is likely, so speaker labels, timestamps and confidence markers travel with the text into coding. Reporting standards are also maturing, with journals and methods guides asking authors to state the model, the correction process and the error rate. The direction of travel is transcripts that carry their own provenance and uncertainty, rather than clean text that hides how it was made.
